3. Plaint case, in short, is that after successive transactions, the suit land measuring about 96 decimals of CS and SA Plot No. 1244 appertaining to CS Khatian No. 212 and SA Khatian No. 507 were owned and possessed by defendant No. 1 and his brother Sudhir Mandai. Then, both of them transferred the suit land to Parul Bal by a registered deed of sale dated 14-5-1969 being deed No. 4400, exhibit 4 and delivered possession. Then, on 4-2-1970 Parul Balal transferred the suit land to one Sufia Khatun by a registered deed of sale being deed No. 1126, exhibit 5 and delivered possession. Sufia Khatun got her name mutated and possessed the suit land for quite some time on payment of rents and then, on 9-12-1977 she transferred by a registered kabala being deed No. 35842, exhibit 7 to Sahabuddin and delivered possession. Then, by about 30 sale deeds exhibit 9 series, Sahabuddin transferred the suit land to the plaintiffs from 1979 to 1984 and delivered possession. The plaintiffs after purchase got their names mutated in respect of their respective land and now, possess the same in their specific share by raising dwelling huts, etc. and on payment of rents. 

 19. The appellate Court appears to have given its all considerations on the title and possession as if it was a suit for declaration of title and possession. It excluded the title deeds of the plaintiffs on the ground that the plaintiffs failed to examine neither the scribe nor the executant of their deeds. But record shows that Sahabuddin who sold the lands to the plaintiffs came before the Court and on oath admitted as PW 4 that he transferred the suit land to the plaintiffs by those sale deeds exhibit 9 series and delivered possession. It rejected the oral evidence of the plaintiffs without considering their entire evidence. It also failed to notice the fact that the plaintiffs have come from various parts of Bangladesh and on different dates purchased the land for the purpose of residence. One of them is not supposed to know every detail of the facts in respect of others. Besides, the notice dated 8-7-1998 issued by the Demra Police, the report of the Advocate Commissioner is the most important evidence on record on possession. When the defendant No.1 claimed the suit land as agricultural land, an Advocate Commissioner was appointed to ascertain the present position and nature of the suit land, namely, whether there is any paddy in the land and also the-number of structures standing thereon. After investigation, the Advocate Commissioner submitted his report on 11-5-1999 with a sketch map. The report was accepted without any objection. Sketch map clearly shows that the entire suit land is divided into plots for residential purposes with a road leading through the middle' of the land for access. Major portion of the land is occupied by different huts. Advocate Commissioner found 8 CI Sheet sheds, 6 semi-pucca and two pucca residential quarters. He definitely reported that he did not find any paddy field. This report together with the sketch map exhibit No.6 belies the case of defendant No.1 that the suit land is a nal land and his borgadar DW-1 cultivates the land with tractor. But such evidence was totally excluded by the appellate Court from consideration on the ground that why the Advocate Commissioner could not say the area of the land or the boundary thereof. The appellate Court failed to notice that such statements were made to questions asked beyond the terms of the reference for investigation, and he had to reply from his memory. Other PWs in chorus stated that the plaintiffs possess the suit land. Against the voluminous documentary evidence of the plaintiffs including rent receipts and RS khatian over a period of about 30 years, the defendant has got not an iota of evidence. But the Court of appeal below found that the plaintiffs do not know the suit land.
